Allosauria.description: Allosauria is a clade of allosauroid theropods comprising Allosauridae and Carcharodontosauria, recovered as the sister group of the metriacanthosaurids within Allosauroidea. The group unites the well-known Late Jurassic Allosaurus with the giant carcharodontosaurians that were among the largest terrestrial predators of the Cretaceous.

Allosauridae.description: Allosauridae is a family of medium to large, bipedal, carnivorous allosauroid theropod dinosaurs from the Late Jurassic, best known from Allosaurus. Their overall anatomy is fairly typical of other theropods, which has long made the family's precise membership difficult to define; Saurophaganax has been attributed to the group, though Danison and colleagues (2024) refer some of its distinguishing elements to a diplodocid sauropod, base a new species of Allosaurus on other material referred to it, and treat Saurophaganax maximus as a nomen dubium. Allosaurid skulls carry prominent horns or hornlets on the lacrimal bones above the eyes that would have been sheathed in keratin, and show marked cranial kinesis, with flexible joints that cushioned the skull and let the animals gape their jaws very wide. Like most theropods they had short forelimbs relative to their hindlimbs, with three-fingered hands bearing long, strongly curved claws suited to raking and grasping prey. The pubis is greatly elongated and ends in a broad "foot" that likely helped support the body's weight when the animal rested in a crouch.

Allosauroidea.description: Allosauroidea is a superfamily of carnosaurian theropod dinosaurs comprising the metriacanthosaurids (sinraptorids), the allosaurids, and the carcharodontosaurians. Its members were among the first giant predators in theropod history, some weighing more than two tons, and together with the megalosauroids they served as apex predators from the Middle Jurassic to the early Late Cretaceous. Fossils have been recovered across North America, South America, Europe, Africa, and Asia, though in North America and Asia allosauroids were eventually replaced by the tyrannosauroids during the Late Cretaceous. These medium- to gigantic-sized bipedal hunters are distinguished by large, narrow skulls roughly two and a half to three times longer than tall, frequently ornamented with crests or rugosities, and by long, laterally compressed, serrated teeth well suited to slicing flesh from prey.

Ankylosauria.description: Ankylosauria is a clade of herbivorous ornithischian dinosaurs that includes the great majority of the armored dinosaurs, whose bodies were sheathed in bony osteoderms much like a turtle's shell. Its members were bulky, low-slung quadrupeds carried on short, powerful limbs. The group first appeared in North Africa during the Middle Jurassic and persisted until the end of the Late Cretaceous. It was traditionally split into the Nodosauridae and the Ankylosauridae, a dichotomy that Raven and colleagues (2023) do not recover. The basal Parankylosauria, known from the latest Cretaceous of southern Gondwana, split from all other ankylosaurs before about 167 million years ago (Soto-Acuña and colleagues, 2021). Together with the plated and spiked stegosaurs, ankylosaurs make up the Thyreophora, the armored branch of ornithischians distinct from the ornithopods and marginocephalians.

Averostra.description: Averostra, meaning "bird snouts," is a clade of theropod dinosaurs within Neotheropoda that encompasses most theropods, uniting the two great branches Ceratosauria and Tetanurae. It represents the only lineage of theropods to survive beyond the Early Jurassic, and so includes nearly every theropod from the Middle Jurassic onward, from the horned ceratosaurs and abelisaurs to the megalosaurs, allosaurs, and the feathered coelurosaurs that ultimately gave rise to birds. Its members are among the most derived theropods, distinguished by the complete loss of the fifth metacarpal, a hand bone that other saurischians retained in reduced form. They also share a promaxillary or maxillary fenestra, an extra opening near the front of the upper jaw, together with fewer teeth in the maxilla, a tooth row set further back along the jaw, and a lacrimal fenestra.

Avetheropoda.description: Avetheropoda is a clade of tetanuran theropod dinosaurs comprising Allosaurus, modern birds, and all descendants of their most recent common ancestor. In effect it unites the two great advanced theropod lineages, the allosauroid carnosaurs and the coelurosaurs, which diverge from one another at the base of the group; it is often treated as equivalent to Neotetanurae (Carrano and colleagues, 2012). Avetheropods account for the bulk of predatory dinosaur diversity of the Late Jurassic and Cretaceous, and they include the only theropods to survive to the present day, the living birds. They are set apart from more basal tetanurans such as the megalosauroids by skeletal details, including a femoral head oriented fully medially rather than anteromedially. The group is recovered in many analyses (Carrano and colleagues, 2012), though Rauhut and colleagues (2024), like some earlier studies, instead unite allosauroids and megalosauroids as Carnosauria.

Bagualosauria.description: Bagualosauria is a clade of sauropodomorph dinosaurs uniting Bagualosaurus with its more derived relatives, including the group Plateosauria and, nested within it, the sauropods. It is the sister lineage to Saturnaliidae, a group of smaller, more basal Carnian sauropodomorphs from South America such as Saturnalia and Chromogisaurus, and Bagualosauria excludes these earliest-diverging forms. Bagualosaurus itself, among the most basal known members of the clade, already shows skull and dental modifications linked to more efficient herbivory along with a moderate increase in body size compared to its saturnaliid relatives, hinting at trends that became far more pronounced later in the group's history. Because it excludes only that earliest-diverging grade, Bagualosauria encompasses most sauropodomorph diversity, ranging from moderate-sized Triassic and Early Jurassic forms to the giant long-necked sauropods of the later Mesozoic.

Carcharodontosauria.description: Carcharodontosauria is a clade of allosauroid theropods comprising Carcharodontosauridae and their closest relatives, encompassing many of the largest terrestrial predators of the Cretaceous across both Gondwana and Laurasia. Its basal members are medium-sized forms that grade into the giant carcharodontosaurids. The carcharodontosaurids underwent a worldwide dispersal during the Early Cretaceous before the family died out in the Turonian, roughly 90 million years ago, after which other large theropods took over the apex-predator role.

Carcharodontosauridae.description: Carcharodontosauridae is a family of giant carnivorous theropod dinosaurs forming a clade within Carnosauria. Its members include some of the largest land predators ever known, among them Acrocanthosaurus, Giganotosaurus, Mapusaurus, and Tyrannotitan, the biggest of which rivaled Tyrannosaurus and Spinosaurus in size, with the heaviest estimated at 8 to 10 metric tons. Together with the spinosaurids, carcharodontosaurids were the dominant large predators of the Early and mid-Cretaceous across Gondwana, and species also occur in North America, Europe, and possibly Asia. Their fossil record spans the Cretaceous from the Barremian to the Turonian, after which they were replaced by smaller abelisaurids in Gondwana and by tyrannosaurids in North America and Asia. Coria and Currie (2006) named a South American subfamily, Giganotosaurinae, for Giganotosaurus and Mapusaurus, which Brusatte and Sereno (2008) replaced with the tribe Giganotosaurini; Carrano and colleagues (2012) found little support for grouping the two genera.

Coelurosauria.description: Coelurosauria is a large and diverse subgroup of theropod dinosaurs, defined as all theropods more closely related to birds than to carnosaurs. It encompasses compsognathids, tyrannosauroids, ornithomimosaurs, and the bird-line maniraptorans, along with megaraptorans, whose exact position remains uncertain. Coelurosaurs range from some of the largest carnivorous dinosaurs, such as Tyrannosaurus, to some of the smallest, and they diversified into omnivorous, insectivorous, herbivorous, and carnivorous forms. Most feathered dinosaurs found so far are coelurosaurs, and many lineages bore filamentous integument or true feathers, though some retained scales over parts of the body. The clade appears by the Middle Jurassic and includes birds, the only dinosaur lineage to survive the end-Cretaceous extinction and the only one alive today.

Dinosauria.description: Dinosauria is a clade of archosaurian reptiles that first appeared early in the Triassic period and went on to become the dominant terrestrial vertebrates for much of the Mesozoic era, through the Jurassic and Cretaceous. The group is extraordinarily diverse, with paleontologists having identified more than 900 genera and over 1,000 species of extinct non-avian dinosaurs alone, ranging from small bipeds to the largest land animals that ever lived, the biggest sauropods reaching nearly 40 meters in length. Dinosaurs share an erect, bird-like leg posture that set them apart from the sprawling stance of most other reptiles, and elaborate display structures such as horns and crests appear across the group, while some lineages evolved bony armor and spines. They were ancestrally bipedal, though many groups became quadrupedal, and the evidence indicates that all laid eggs, with nest-building widespread. Birds are the one dinosaur lineage to have survived the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction roughly 66 million years ago, so the clade is divided into the avian dinosaurs (birds) and the extinct non-avian dinosaurs.

Eutyrannosauria.description: Eutyrannosauria is a clade of large-bodied tyrannosauroid theropod dinosaurs of the Northern Hemisphere, encompassing the family Tyrannosauridae together with its closest non-tyrannosaurid relatives, such as the eastern North American genera Dryptosaurus and Appalachiosaurus (Voris and colleagues, 2025). The southwestern North American Bistahieversor is the sister of Tyrannosauridae in the analysis of Delcourt and Grillo (2018) but falls within Tyrannosaurinae in that of Voris and colleagues (2025). It was defined to set these advanced, often gigantic northern forms apart from the more basal, globally distributed tyrannosauroids. Members are distinguished by their great size and by prominent cranial ornamentation, including roughened, ridge-bearing nasal bones. Powers and colleagues (2026) instead recover a family Dryptosauridae, including Dryptosaurus, in all their implied-weights analyses.

Genasauria.description: Genasauria is a clade that encompasses the great majority of ornithischian dinosaurs, excluding only the earliest-diverging forms such as Lesothosaurus. It unites two major branches: Thyreophora, the armored dinosaurs including ankylosaurs, stegosaurs, and more primitive relatives like Scelidosaurus; and Cerapoda, which gathers the ornithopods, ceratopsians, pachycephalosaurs, and various small early forms. Members were primarily herbivores that typically held their heads about a meter off the ground, suggesting they fed mainly on ground-level plants such as ferns, cycads, and other low-growing gymnosperms. A hallmark of the group is the presence of fleshy cheeks bounding inset tooth rows, an adaptation for more efficient processing of plant material in the mouth.

Massopoda.description: Massopoda is a clade of sauropodomorph dinosaurs that lived from the Late Triassic through the Late Cretaceous. It is defined as all sauropodomorphs more closely related to Saltasaurus than to Plateosaurus (Yates, 2007), and its name is a contraction of Massospondylidae and Sauropoda, two very different groups that both fall within it. Nested inside is the more exclusive Sauropodiformes, the most inclusive group that contains Saltasaurus but excludes Massospondylus (McPhee and colleagues, 2014). Its members range from small, bipedal massospondylids to the gigantic, quadrupedal true sauropods, and together they encompass the great majority of sauropodomorph diversity.

Massospondylidae.description: Massospondylidae is a family of early massopod sauropodomorph dinosaurs that lived from the Late Triassic to the Early Jurassic, with a near-global spread that reached Asia, Africa, North America, South America, and Antarctica. It is defined as a stem-based group encompassing all animals more closely related to Massospondylus carinatus than to Plateosaurus or Saltasaurus (Sereno, 2007). Most recent analyses recover a monophyletic Massospondylidae that usually includes Massospondylus, Coloradisaurus and Lufengosaurus with a variable number of other taxa, though some have found it to contain Massospondylus alone (Barrett and colleagues, 2019); Fernández and Werneburg (2022) add Adeopapposaurus, Glacialisaurus and Leyesaurus, and Pradhania falls within the family for Novas and colleagues (2010) but in Unaysauridae for Barrett and colleagues (2026). Its members were small to medium-sized, long-necked, facultatively bipedal herbivores or omnivores that represent an early-branching lineage of sauropodomorphs rather than close relatives of the true sauropods.

Neotheropoda.description: Neotheropoda, meaning "new theropods," is a clade that encompasses nearly all theropod dinosaurs, from the small, lightly built coelophysoids of the Late Triassic to the more advanced ceratosaurs and tetanurans, the latter of which ultimately gave rise to modern birds. Its members are distinguished by a reduction of several foot bones, which left the characteristic three-toed (tridactyl) footprints associated with theropods. It is the only group of theropods to survive the Triassic-Jurassic extinction event, after which it radiated into the dominant terrestrial predators of the Jurassic and Cretaceous. The more derived members form the clade Averostra, which unites the ceratosaurs and the tetanurans; by the Early Jurassic the non-averostran lineages had died out.

Nodosauridae.description: Nodosauridae is a family of armored, quadrupedal, herbivorous ankylosaurian dinosaurs known from the Late Jurassic to the Late Cretaceous of Asia, Europe, North America, and possibly South America. Like their close relatives the ankylosaurids, nodosaurids were heavily built and clad in rows of bony nodules and spines set into the skin and sheathed in keratin, but they lacked the mace-like bony tail club of the ankylosaurids and instead retained a more flexible tail. Many bore prominent spikes projecting outward from the neck and shoulders, and they carried a narrower, more elongate skull than the broad-headed ankylosaurids. The family is traditionally composed of the spiny, basal polacanthines, together with the panoplosaurine and struthiosaurine lineages of the more derived Nodosaurinae. One exceptionally preserved nodosaurid, the "mummy" of Borealopelta, retains its armor in life position along with keratin and skin traces that record a reddish, countershaded coloration.

dispute.summary: The monophyly of Nodosauridae is contested. It is the traditional, broadly used family for non-tail-clubbed ankylosaurs, but Raven and colleagues (2023) recovered it as paraphyletic, with separate panoplosaurid, polacanthid and struthiosaurid radiations, for which they defined the existing names Panoplosauridae, Polacanthidae and Struthiosauridae; the basal polacanthine taxa (Polacanthus, Hylaeosaurus, Gastonia, Hoplitosaurus) variously fall within or outside it across analyses. The traditional Nodosauridae is retained pending broad consensus.

Ornithischia.description: Ornithischia, meaning "bird-hipped," is one of the two great branches of dinosaurs, encompassing a mostly herbivorous radiation whose members are known from every continent and across an enormous range of sizes. The group takes its name from a pelvis superficially resembling that of birds, though this is a case of convergence, since birds are in fact theropods and only distantly related. Its major subgroups include the horn-faced ceratopsians, the thick-domed pachycephalosaurs, the armored thyreophorans such as stegosaurs and ankylosaurs, and the ornithopods, alongside a scattering of small, early-diverging forms near the base of the group. The earliest members were lightly built bipeds around one to two meters long with long counterbalancing tails, but later lineages grew far larger and many became quadrupedal. Most were browsers or grazers of ground-level plants, though a few were opportunistic omnivores. Several ornithischians are known to have lived in herds, sometimes with juveniles flocking apart from adults, and exceptionally preserved specimens reveal a range of skin coverings from mosaic scales to disputed filamentous, quill-like structures.

Plateosauria.description: Plateosauria is a large, node-based clade within Sauropodomorpha, conventionally defined as the last common ancestor of Plateosaurus and Massospondylus (Sereno, 2007), or of Plateosaurus and Jingshanosaurus (Galton and Upchurch, 2004), together with all of that ancestor's descendants. So defined, it unites the Plateosauridae with the more inclusive Massopoda and takes in Late Triassic and Early Jurassic sauropodomorphs such as Coloradisaurus, Euskelosaurus, Jingshanosaurus, Massospondylus, Mussaurus, Sellosaurus, and Yunnanosaurus, while its descendant lineages also encompass the giant, long-necked true sauropods. It groups the more derived, generally herbivorous members of the lineage, spanning the transition from largely bipedal early forms toward larger-bodied, increasingly quadrupedal ones. In all, it accounts for the bulk of sauropodomorph diversity above the earliest, most basal grade.

Saurischia.description: Saurischia, meaning "lizard-hipped," is one of the two major divisions of dinosaurs, distinguished from the ornithischians by hip structure. Its members retain the ancestral, three-pronged pelvic arrangement in which the pubis points forward, the same configuration seen in modern lizards and other reptiles, rather than the backward-rotated pubis of ornithischians. The group encompasses the mostly carnivorous, typically bipedal theropods together with the long-necked, herbivorous sauropodomorphs, and because birds are a lineage of maniraptoran theropods, they too fall within Saurischia. It is defined as birds and all dinosaurs more closely related to them than to Triceratops (Sereno, 1998); Gauthier (1986) had defined it against Ornithischia as a whole. All saurischians except birds died out in the Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction event at the end of the Cretaceous, while birds survive as the clade's only living descendants.

Sauropodomorpha.description: Sauropodomorpha is a clade of saurischian dinosaurs that includes the long-necked, herbivorous sauropods together with their earlier relatives, the basal forms traditionally grouped as "prosauropods." The clade first appeared among the earliest dinosaurs in the Late Triassic, around 230 million years ago, and persisted until the end-Cretaceous extinction. Its earliest members were small bipeds that were omnivorous or even carnivorous, but over time the group shifted toward plant-eating, larger body size, and, in the true sauropods, quadrupedal locomotion. The sauropods became the dominant terrestrial herbivores through much of the Mesozoic and include the largest animals ever to walk on land. Their remains have been found on every continent, including Antarctica.

Tetanurae.description: Tetanurae, meaning "stiff tails," is a large clade of theropod dinosaurs that includes most predatory dinosaur diversity, encompassing the megalosauroids, the allosauroids, and the coelurosaurs, the last of which contains tyrannosauroids, ornithomimosaurs, compsognathids, and the maniraptorans, including living birds. The group is defined as all theropods more closely related to modern birds than to Ceratosauria (Gauthier, 1986), its sister lineage, from which it diverged during the Late Triassic according to Sereno and colleagues (1994). Tetanurans appear in the fossil record by the Early Jurassic and had become globally distributed by the Middle Jurassic. Their evolution was marked by the parallel diversification of several lineages that repeatedly attained large body size and similar locomotor forms; basal members were the first theropods to reach truly giant sizes, with some megalosauroids and allosauroids exceeding a ton. Distinctive features of the group include stiffened tails, the loss of the fourth finger to leave a three-fingered hand, maxillary teeth restricted to the front of the snout, and, in more advanced forms, an air-sac-ventilated lung system resembling that of modern birds. Birds are the only living survivors of the clade.

Theropoda.description: Theropoda is one of the three major clades of dinosaurs, alongside Ornithischia and Sauropodomorpha, and is generally grouped among the saurischians as a nearer relative of the sauropodomorphs. Theropods were ancestrally carnivorous and included the majority of large terrestrial predators from the Early Jurassic until the end of the Cretaceous, among them the largest meat-eating land animals ever to exist, such as Tyrannosaurus and Giganotosaurus. First appearing in the Late Triassic, the group spans an enormous range of body sizes and lifestyles, with several lineages independently shifting to herbivory or omnivory. Its major subgroups include the early coelophysoids and the often horned ceratosaurs, together with the sprawling tetanuran radiation, which encompasses the semiaquatic spinosaurids, the allosauroids, and the feathered coelurosaurs, the last including tyrannosaurids, ornithomimosaurs, dromaeosaurids, and therizinosaurs. From small, specialized coelurosaurs, birds arose during the Jurassic and endure today as roughly 11,000 living species, making theropods the only dinosaur lineage still present on Earth.

Thyreophora.description: Thyreophora, meaning "shield bearers," is a clade of armored ornithischian dinosaurs. It contains two major subgroups, the plated stegosaurs and the heavily armored ankylosaurs, together with a grade of early-diverging forms such as Scutellosaurus, Emausaurus, and Scelidosaurus. Its members are defined by body armor arranged in longitudinal rows along the back and flanks: primitive forms bore simple low keeled scutes, while more derived members developed elaborate spikes and plates. Thyreophorans first appeared in the Early Jurassic and persisted until the end of the Cretaceous. The earliest species were small and at least partly bipedal, but the group trended toward a robust, low-slung body plan, with the large stegosaurs and ankylosaurs becoming obligate quadrupeds whose forelimbs were much shorter than their hindlimbs.

Tyrannosauridae.description: Tyrannosauridae is a family of coelurosaurian theropod dinosaurs that lived near the end of the Cretaceous period, with fossils known only from North America and Asia. It is divided into two subfamilies: the more lightly built Albertosaurinae, comprising the North American genera Albertosaurus and Gorgosaurus, and the Tyrannosaurinae, which includes Daspletosaurus, Tarbosaurus, Teratophoneus, Zhuchengtyrannus, and Tyrannosaurus itself, among others. Estimates of how many genera the family contains range from as few as three to around fifteen. Though descended from smaller ancestors, tyrannosaurids were almost always the largest predators in their ecosystems, standing at the apex of the food chain. They were bipedal carnivores with massive, deep skulls packed with large teeth, proportionally long and cursorial hindlimbs for their size, and greatly reduced forelimbs bearing only two functional fingers.

Tyrannosaurinae.description: Tyrannosaurinae is one of the two subfamilies of tyrannosaurid theropods, known from Late Cretaceous deposits of western North America and east Asia. Compared with their albertosaurine relatives, tyrannosaurines were generally more robust, larger, and more heavily built, with deep, powerful skulls; the exceptions were the long-snouted, more gracile alioramins. The group includes some of the oldest tyrannosaurids, such as Lythronax, alongside its youngest and most famous member, Tyrannosaurus rex. Its genera are usually sorted into several lineages: the basal Alioramini, the American southwestern Teratophoneini, and a group uniting the Daspletosaurini and the Tyrannosaurini, which contains Tarbosaurus and Tyrannosaurus. Studies of Tyrannosaurus growth suggest these animals changed markedly with age, shifting from slender, semi-long-snouted juveniles into robust, heavy-headed adults that likely occupied different ecological niches as they matured.

Tyrannosauroidea.description: Tyrannosauroidea is a superfamily of coelurosaurian theropod dinosaurs that unites the family Tyrannosauridae with a range of smaller, more basal relatives such as the proceratosaurids. The group arose on the northern supercontinent Laurasia in the Jurassic and persisted until the end of the Cretaceous, when tyrannosauroids became the dominant large predators of the Northern Hemisphere, culminating in the giant Tyrannosaurus; their fossils are known from what are now North America, Europe, and Asia. All members were bipedal carnivores distinguished by a suite of skull and pelvic features, including a tall premaxilla that blunted the front of the snout, fused and often roughly textured nasal bones, and small, D-shaped premaxillary teeth. Early forms were small animals with long, three-fingered forelimbs, whereas the later giants reached enormous size yet had proportionately tiny, two-fingered arms; the derived forms also developed a pinched third metatarsal, the arctometatarsus, tied to running efficiency. Primitive filamentous feathers are preserved in several species, and many tyrannosauroids bore bony crests of varied shape on the skull that likely served for display.

Acrocanthosaurus.description: Acrocanthosaurus is a genus of carcharodontosaurid dinosaurs that existed in what is now North America during the Barremian and early Cenomanian stages of the Early Cretaceous and Late Cretaceous, from 125 to 99.6 million years ago. Like most dinosaur genera, Acrocanthosaurus contains only a single species, A. atokensis. It had a continent-wide range, with fossil remains known from the U.S. states of Oklahoma, Texas, and Wyoming in the west and Maryland in the east. However, most of these remains are assigned to the species based on the assumption that Acrocanthosaurus is the only large carcharodontosaurid from North America during this time, and the possibility exists that some referred specimens could represent distinct taxa.

Allosaurus.etymology: From Greek 'allos' meaning 'different' or 'other' and 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'; meaning 'different lizard', alluding to its lightweight vertebrae
Allosaurus.description: Allosaurus is a genus of theropod dinosaur that lived 155 to 145 million years ago during the Late Jurassic period (Kimmeridgian to late Tithonian ages). The first fossil remains that could definitively be ascribed to this genus were described in 1877 by Othniel C. Marsh. The name "Allosaurus" means "different lizard", alluding to its lightweight vertebrae, which Marsh believed were unique. The genus has a very complicated taxonomy and includes at least three valid species, the best known of which is A. fragilis. The bulk of Allosaurus remains come from North America's Morrison Formation, with material also known from the Alcobaça, Bombarral, and Lourinhã formations in Portugal. It was known for over half of the 20th century as Antrodemus, but a study of the abundant remains from the Cleveland-Lloyd Dinosaur Quarry returned the name "Allosaurus" to prominence. As one of the first well-known theropod dinosaurs, it has long attracted attention outside of paleontological circles.
diagnostic_features: Vertebral centra deeply excavated on the sides to reduce weight, producing an hourglass form in some elements
Vertebrae biconcave with shallow cavities, centra not pneumatic but greatly lightened by lateral excavations

Daspletosaurus.etymology: From Greek daspletos ('frightful') + sauros ('lizard'), meaning 'frightful lizard'.
Daspletosaurus.description: Daspletosaurus is a genus of tyrannosaurid dinosaur that lived in Laramidia between about 77 and 74.4 million years ago, during the Late Cretaceous Period. The genus Daspletosaurus contains three named species. Fossils of the earlier type species, D. torosus, have been found in Alberta, while fossils of a later species, D. horneri, have been found in Montana and Alberta. D. wilsoni has been suggested as an intermediate species between D. torosus and D. horneri that evolved through anagenesis, though further research may be required to definitively support the theory.
diagnostic_features: Premaxilla does not contact nasal below external naris.
Lacrimal 'horn' triangular in lateral aspect, with apex centered above antorbital ramus of bone; exceeds postorbital 'horn' in development.
Neural spine of fourth cervical vertebra much larger than that of fifth; spine of fifth distally pointed.
In adults humerus length estimated equal to 38 per cent of femur length; forelimb powerfully developed.
Anterodistal condyle of metacarpal I reduced, causing first digit to diverge distally from second.
In adults circumference of femur equals 38 to 41 per cent of femur length.

Pneumatic foramen penetrating the lateral surface of the quadratojugal.
Humerus about 34% the length of the femur.

Nanotyrannus.etymology: Originally proposed by Bakker, Williams and Currie (1988) as Latin nano ("small") plus tyrannus ("tyrant"); the derivation is now usually corrected to Greek nanos ("dwarf" or "pygmy") and tyrannos ("king"), in reference to the small body size relative to other tyrannosauroids.
Nanotyrannus.description: Nanotyrannus is a genus of tyrannosauroid dinosaur that lived in what is now western North America during the Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous, 67 to 66 million years ago. Its fossils are known from the Hell Creek Formation. It was one of the last-known non-avian dinosaurs and lived until the Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction event. The first named species, N. lancensis, was described as a new species of Gorgosaurus in 1946 by Charles W. Gilmore based on a single skull. Re-examination of the specimen in 1988 by Robert T. Bakker, Michael Williams and Philip J. Currie moved the species to a new genus of tyrannosaurid, named Nanotyrannus in reference to its small body size compared to other tyrannosaurids.

dispute.summary: The validity of Nanotyrannus is actively contested. After the 1988 erection of the genus, Carr (1999) and Woodward and colleagues (2020) argued that the holotype CMNH 7541 is an immature Tyrannosaurus rex, citing tooth-grain immaturity and femoral osteohistology. Longrich and Saitta (2024), Zanno and Napoli (2025) — who erected a second species, N. lethaeus — and Griffin and colleagues (2025, ceratobranchial histology) reaffirmed Nanotyrannus as a distinct, skeletally mature taxon. No broad consensus yet.

Extraordinarily wide basicranium between basitubera and basipterygoid processes.
Two large pneumatic foramina placed one behind the other near the midline of the basisphenoid.
Dorsal surface of the nasal lacks strong ridges and striae.
Parietal wing of the occiput with a sharp angle between dorsal and lateral edges.
Basicranial boxwork with flat ventral floor.

Tarbosaurus.etymology: From Ancient Greek 'tarbos' meaning 'terror' or 'alarm' and 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Tarbosaurus.description: Tarbosaurus is a genus of large tyrannosaurid dinosaur that lived in Asia during the Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous epoch. It contains the type and single species Tarbosaurus bataar, which is known from the Nemegt Formation of Mongolia, with more fragmentary remains found further afield in the Subashi Formation of China. Tarbosaurus is represented by dozens of fossil specimens, including several complete skulls and skeletons. These remains have allowed studies focusing on its phylogeny, skull mechanics, and brain structure. Further fossil remains have been reported from other geologic formations of Asia, however, these remains are fragmentary and cannot be confidently assigned to Tarbosaurus or the type species.

dispute.summary: The generic placement of the single Mongolian species is long debated. Maleev (1955) named the type material Tyrannosaurus bataar (holotype PIN 551-1) and, in a companion paper, erected Tarbosaurus for the related Tarbosaurus efremovi. Rozhdestvensky (1965) interpreted Maleev's several Mongolian species as growth stages of one animal and, keeping the genus Tarbosaurus, coined the combination Tarbosaurus bataar. Carpenter (1992) judged the differences from Tyrannosaurus to fall within normal individual and ontogenetic variation and sank Tarbosaurus into Tyrannosaurus (Tyrannosaurus bataar), whereas Olshevsky, Ford and Yamamoto (1995) instead split the material among Tarbosaurus, Jenghizkhan and Maleevosaurus. Most work since 1999 recognizes a single species; the majority retains Tarbosaurus bataar, with a minority (e.g. Carr and others) treating it as Tyrannosaurus bataar.

Tyrannosaurus.etymology: From Greek tyrannos (tyrant) and sauros (lizard); meaning "tyrant lizard", a name Osborn coined to convey the genus's exceptional size relative to all then-known carnivorous land vertebrates.
Tyrannosaurus.description: Tyrannosaurus is a genus of large theropod dinosaur. The type species Tyrannosaurus rex (rex meaning 'king' in Latin), often shortened to T. rex, is one of the best represented theropods. It lived throughout what is now western North America, on what was then an island continent known as Laramidia, and had a much wider range than other tyrannosaurids. Fossils are found in a variety of geological formations dated to the late Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous period, 69 to 66 million years ago, with isolated specimens possibly indicating an earlier origin in the middle Campanian age. It was one of the last known members of the tyrannosaurids and among the last non-avian dinosaurs to exist before the Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction event.
diagnostic_features: Megalocephalic skull with deep, massively built proportions, brought close to the sacrum by a shortened presacral column of approximately 23 vertebrae.
Fused nasals forming an arched midline ridge on the snout that reinforces the skull against bite-induced stress.
Teeth heterodont and broadly oval to D-shaped in cross-section, with transverse diameter exceeding anteroposterior; alveolar reinforcing plates on the inner surface of the maxilla and dentary.
Squamosal bearing a distinctive horizontal anterior bar projecting into the laterotemporal fenestra.
Forelimb extremely reduced; functionally didactyl manus with powerful recurved unguals; humerus little more than half the length of the femur.
Five sacral vertebrae coossified into a single neural plate with three small fenestrations between S2 and S5.
Pubis, ilium and ischium firmly coalesced; pubis terminating distally in a hugely expanded pedicle ("pubic boot").
Caudal series of approximately 53 vertebrae forming a long, flexible balancing tail without the rod-like rigidity of ornithomimids.

The second most complete Tyrannosaurus skeleton, 199 bones representing 70 percent of the total, from the Hell Creek Formation. Its pathologies include broken and healed ribs, a broken and healed neck, and a hole in the back of the head about the size of a Tyrannosaurus tooth.

Reported to measure 13 meters in length. Using a mass estimation technique extrapolating from femur circumference, Scotty was estimated as the largest known Tyrannosaurus specimen at 8.87 t in body mass.

From the Hell Creek Formation. Yielded medullary tissue in its femur, found only in female birds during ovulation, confirming it as a female that died during ovulation; the only Tyrannosaurus conclusively sexed. Also a source of reported soft-tissue blood vessels and collagen.

notable_specimens.institution: Houston Museum of Nature and Science
notable_specimens.significance: Preserves patches of mosaic scales on the tail, hip, and neck, used in a 2017 review concluding that feather covering of large tyrannosaurids, if present, was limited to the upper side of the trunk. Also shows pathologies: a hole penetrating its jugal and severe tail trauma with bone remodeling.

The first complete Tyrannosaurus forelimbs were identified in 1989 belonging to MOR 555, confirming that the genus had short two-fingered arms about 1 meter long, as had been suggested from the related Gorgosaurus.
